content: Okay. So. Something happened this week that I'm still trying to process. The Asahi Shimbun Weekly — the food section — published a review of Osteria Morishita. March 19, 2026. Hiroko Sano wrote it. I found out when my phone started going insane on Thursday morning and I couldn't figure out why. I had to have my sister-in-law read the headline to me because I literally couldn't look at the screen.
That's the kind of moment that freezes you. What did the headline say?

"Azabu's Quiet Modena: A Trattoria With Conviction." That's the headline. I've read it probably forty times now and it still doesn't feel real. Hiroko Sano. She's the one who more or less made Sato's reputation in Roppongi, she destroyed that fusion place in Ginza with three paragraphs, and she wrote about us. About the ragu bolognese. About the wine list. About what she called our "unfussy precision." I keep saying those words to myself: unfussy precision. That's it. That's everything I've been trying to do for three years.

"Unfussy precision" — honestly, that's a remarkable phrase for a critic to land on. It captures something really specific. It's not calling you refined in a way that sounds cold, and it's not calling you rustic in a way that sounds like an excuse. It's saying you know exactly what you're doing and you refuse to perform it. The ragu bolognese being mentioned by name — that's not accidental either. Sano tends to anchor her pieces in the dish she thinks most honestly represents the kitchen's philosophy. The fact that she chose that one specifically tells you something about what she understood when she was there.

How are you feeling right now, a couple of days after? Past the initial shock of it?

Honestly? Terrified. Because reservation requests spiked 4x in 48 hours. Forty-eight hours. We went from our normal inquiry volume to four times that, and it hasn't slowed down. I'm booked 3 weeks out for Friday and Saturday dinner now. Three weeks. That's never happened. We've had busy stretches before, a good mention here and there, but nothing like this. And now I'm sitting here looking at my team of seven — six plus me — and thinking: what do I actually do with this?

That's the question underneath all of this, isn't it. The review didn't just bring you attention — it brought you a very specific kind of attention from people who read Hiroko Sano because they trust her judgment about exactly the kind of restaurant you are. Which means they're coming in with real expectations. They want to find what she described. And what she described is something that is, by its nature, difficult to scale without losing the thing that earned the description in the first place.

Before we talk about what to do operationally, I want to ask: what does your gut tell you is the biggest vulnerability right now? If you imagine a table of four coming in on a Friday night three weeks from now, what's the thing in the current operation that worries you most under pressure?

The ragu. I know that sounds strange given that it's the dish she named. But maybe it's not strange — maybe it's exactly because she named it. The ragu bolognese takes four hours minimum. My sous chef Takashi handles it on weekdays but I do it on Friday and Saturday nights personally, and I've always considered that a feature, not a bug. When we're doing forty covers, that's manageable. If I'm looking at fifty-five or sixty covers on a Friday, and the ragu is one of the primary things people are coming specifically to eat, I'm scared we run short, we feel rushed, or — and this is the real nightmare — the ragu becomes the thing that defines us and I can't keep doing it personally at that volume without something else slipping.

The wine list is the other thing. Sano mentioned it. I curate it myself, everything is imported through two small importers I've worked with for years, and almost nothing on the list is what you'd find anywhere else in Tokyo. That takes time. The moment I start needing to fill gaps fast, the list becomes generic, and then we're just another place with a decent pasta.

You've named two things that are both real and interconnected, and I think it's worth separating them clearly so you can think about each without conflating them.

The ragu bolognese problem is ultimately a throughput and attention problem. The dish takes four hours, you've been doing it personally on high-volume nights, and demand has now shifted in a way that could break that rhythm. There are a few honest paths here, and none of them is cost-free. One is to keep the ragu exactly as it is, keep it on the menu, but treat it as a limited quantity item — you make what you can make correctly, and when it's gone, it's gone. You communicate that clearly, not as a failure but as a fact. Some tables won't get it on a given night. That preserves the dish but changes the experience for some guests. Another path is to bring Takashi fully into the Friday-Saturday ragu process alongside you — not replacing you, but building a real shared protocol so the execution can hold at higher volume. That requires an honest conversation with Takashi about whether he's ready for that responsibility, and it requires you to truly codify what makes your version what it is, which is actually a useful exercise regardless. A third path, which I'd be cautious about but worth naming, is to rotate the ragu out as a nightly special rather than a standing menu item, which protects it from becoming a production problem but risks disappointing exactly the people who came because Sano mentioned it by name.

The wine list problem is different in kind. It's a sourcing and relationship problem. The vulnerability you're describing isn't really about volume — it's about what happens when your existing importers can't keep up with the new pace of consumption, and you find yourself making reactive purchasing decisions. The way to protect against that is actually to have the conversation with your two importers now, before you feel the pressure. Tell them what happened. Tell them what the next three months might look like. Ask them honestly what their constraints are. That conversation will tell you whether your current relationships can hold, or whether you need to think carefully about adding a third importer — someone who shares the same sourcing philosophy — rather than reaching for convenience bottles when you're in a pinch.

Do either of those feel like the right place to start thinking?

The ragu one. Definitely. And actually your framing of those three paths is helpful because I've been going in circles on it. I think the limited quantity approach has something right about it, but I'm worried about the message it sends. If someone comes in specifically because they read "Azabu's Quiet Modena: A Trattoria With Conviction" — Hiroko Sano's piece — and they've waited three weeks to get a table, and they sit down and the ragu is already sold out at eight o'clock... that feels like a broken promise. Even if it's an honest one.

But the idea of trying to scale it to sixty covers without bringing Takashi into the process properly scares me more. I've watched other chefs try to just push through on volume and you can taste it. Something gets hollowed out. I don't want to be that restaurant six months after a good review.

You're right to worry about the sold-out-at-eight scenario. That's not a charming constraint if it's discovered at the table — it's a disappointment with no good recovery. But I think there's a version of the limited quantity approach that actually works if you build it into the reservation flow rather than revealing it at service.

Consider this: when people book a Friday or Saturday dinner reservation — especially now that you're 3 weeks out for those nights — you include a brief note in the confirmation that describes the ragu as a dish prepared in limited quantity each evening, and suggests, without hard-selling it, that guests who have a particular interest in it mention it when they arrive so you can let them know availability. That changes the dynamic completely. The constraint becomes part of the story of the restaurant, which is consistent with everything Sano was writing about. It communicates that you don't industrialize things. It also gives you useful information at the start of service about how many tables specifically want it, which helps Takashi and your floor team sequence the night better.

This also opens a door to something else: what if the ragu were plated slightly differently on Friday and Saturday? Not a different dish — the same preparation, same care — but presented in a way that acknowledges its central role. Not in a showy way. In a way that's honest. A small written card at the table, a word from the server about the cook time and the sourcing of the meat, something that makes the experience of getting the ragu feel intentional rather than incidental. That's not theater. That's hospitality.

On Takashi — can I ask, what's your honest read of him? Not as a technician, but as someone who understands what you're building. Because the codification question — actually writing down your ragu bolognese protocol in enough detail that someone else can hold the standard — that's not just a practical necessity at this moment. It's also a test of whether you've articulated to yourself what you actually care about. Chefs who struggle most with scaling are often chefs who know what they want instinctively but haven't translated that into language someone else can execute.

That's a real question and it deserves an honest answer. Takashi has been with me since we opened. He was with me before that, actually — he was at the place in Sangenjaya where I spent two years really figuring out what I wanted Osteria Morishita to be. He understands the philosophy. He knows why we don't rush the soffritto. He's the one who pushed back on me when I was tempted to use pre-made pasta for a week in 2024 when we had a staffing crisis — he actually said, "If we do that, what are we?" So he gets it.

But there's a difference between getting it and being ready to own it when I'm not there. And I think part of why I've kept the Friday-Saturday ragu for myself isn't really about trust in Takashi. It's that I haven't been ready to let go of it. It's the dish that most feels like me. The ragu bolognese is basically my argument for why I exist as a chef. And handing that to someone else, even someone I trust completely, feels like something I haven't emotionally prepared for.

Maybe Sano's review is forcing that conversation, even though she doesn't know it.

That's a remarkably clear piece of self-knowledge. And I think you're right — the review is forcing the conversation, but the conversation was always coming. It just needed a catalyst with enough weight behind it.

Here's what I'd offer, for what it's worth: what you're describing with Takashi isn't actually a transfer of authorship. It's more like a translation. You've been carrying the ragu bolognese as something almost pre-verbal — you know it in your hands, in the timing, in the sound of the soffritto at the right moment. The act of codifying it, of sitting down with Takashi and cooking it together and talking through every decision out loud, isn't giving it away. It's actually the first time you'll have fully understood what you've been doing. Cooks who work from deep intuition often discover, when forced to articulate it, that they know more than they thought they knew — and that the articulation itself makes the dish more stable, not less alive.

The emotional preparation you mentioned — I don't think you can think your way into it ahead of time. You probably just have to do it. Schedule a Tuesday morning, no service pressure, cook the ragu with Takashi from scratch, and narrate every choice. Record it if that helps. See what happens when you try to say out loud why you add the wine when you do, why the meat goes in at the temperature it goes in, what you're smelling for. Takashi already knows the philosophy. He told you so in 2024. Now you're giving him the language to carry it.

What does the rest of your team look like on the floor side? Because the surge in demand you're describing — the 4x spike in reservation requests, being fully booked 3 weeks out on weekends — that's a kitchen pressure but it's also an enormous floor pressure. How many covers can your dining room actually hold well, and what's it going to feel like when you're pushing against that ceiling every Friday and Saturday for the foreseeable future?

The dining room seats thirty-eight. That's the capacity. We've never done more than forty-four with bar seating on a truly packed night, and forty-four felt like too many — I could feel it. The pacing got choppy, the servers were covering too much, the sense of calm that I consider essential to what we're doing just... started to thin.

I have three servers. Miho, who has been with me since the beginning and could run the room in her sleep. Kenji, who has been with us about eighteen months and is very good but still learning the wine knowledge in the depth I want. And then we added Natsuki six months ago, she came from a kaiseki background and her table presence is exceptional but she's still internalizing the Italian wine specifics that matter for our list.

So thirty-eight covers with Miho, Kenji, and Natsuki — that's workable. That's actually quite good on a good night. But here's the uncomfortable truth: the demand we're looking at now means that people who couldn't get a Friday or Saturday reservation are going to push into Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday. And those nights I've historically been a bit looser, a bit more casual, maybe thirty covers, less pressure. Now suddenly those midweek nights might feel like what Friday used to feel like, and I'm not sure the staffing reflects that.

That's the pressure wave you really need to think about. The weekend problem is visible and immediate — you can see it in the reservation book, you can plan for it, you know it's coming. The midweek problem is more insidious because it'll arrive gradually and then all at once. You'll have a Tuesday where you're at thirty-two covers with the same staffing that used to handle twenty-six, and by ten o'clock you'll notice something felt off but you won't be able to name exactly what.

A few things worth thinking through on the floor side.

Kenji's wine knowledge is the gap that surfaces most directly from Sano's review. She mentioned the wine list. That means guests who come because of the review will have read that sentence, and some of them will ask questions — not to be difficult, but because they're genuinely curious about what you've built. Kenji being uncertain in that moment is a real problem, not a catastrophic one, but one that erodes exactly the confidence the review created. The question is how you close that gap quickly enough to matter. You might consider dedicating twenty minutes before service, two or three nights a week, specifically to wine conversation — not tasting necessarily, but narrating. You, or Miho, walking through three or four bottles and talking about why they're on the list, what they're doing next to the food, what the importer relationship is. Make it a habit rather than a curriculum.

On the midweek staffing — you have a few honest options. You could bring in a part-time fourth server for the nights that start filling up, someone with enough experience that they don't need hand-holding, even if their Italian wine depth isn't there yet, because Miho can anchor those nights. Alternatively, you look at whether your reservation caps on weeknights need to adjust upward slightly, just to reflect the new reality, which means your existing team needs to stretch a little — which is a different cost. Or you hold the midweek cap at roughly what it's been, accept that the demand overflow will simply create a waiting list, and treat that as an asset rather than a problem.

The last option actually interests me for your situation. You are now, because of Hiroko Sano, a restaurant that people are willing to wait for. That's not a burden — that's a position. The question is whether you manage from that position or let the pressure of the demand manage you.

What's your instinct on the cap? Do you have a number that you feel is the honest limit of what you can do well — not your best night, but your sustainable excellent night?

Thirty-eight. That's the number. And I know it sounds like I'm just citing the room capacity but it's not that — it's actually that thirty-eight is where I feel like every table gets what it should get. The food comes out right, the floor has time to actually talk to people, I'm not watching the clock in the kitchen the way I start watching it at forty-two. Thirty-eight is where we're honest.

I think that's what I want to hold. And I think — and this is something I'm deciding as I say it — I think I want to use this moment to formalize that. Not apologetically, not as a limitation, but as a statement. We seat thirty-eight. That's the restaurant. Hiroko Sano wrote about a certain kind of place, and that place has thirty-eight seats, and if you want to eat there you'll wait three weeks for a Friday, and that's what it means. I think I've been slightly embarrassed by the smallness of what we are, and I think that review just told me I shouldn't be.

I'm going to call my importer tomorrow about the wine. I'm going to cook the ragu with Takashi on Tuesday. And I think I need to write something short — just a paragraph — for the website and for the reservation confirmation, something that says who we are now that more people are paying attention. Not a manifesto. Just an honest description.

That clarity is worth everything. You moved from processing shock to an actual set of decisions in one conversation, and the decisions are coherent — they all point in the same direction. You're not trying to become a different restaurant. You're trying to become a more fully realized version of the restaurant you already are.

The paragraph for the website and reservation confirmation — I'd offer a few thoughts on what makes it land and what makes it sound like marketing. The things that make it land: it's specific rather than generic, it uses the language of fact rather than aspiration, it doesn't promise an experience so much as describe a reality. The things that kill it: phrases like "intimate dining" or "carefully sourced ingredients" or "passion for Italian cuisine" — any language that could describe any restaurant in Tokyo without anyone noticing. What you're writing is not for people who haven't heard of you. It's for people who just read that Hiroko Sano described your ragu bolognese and your wine list and your unfussy precision, and who want to know what they're walking into before they arrive.

Something that might be worth including, without being prescriptive about the exact wording: that the restaurant seats thirty-eight. That the ragu bolognese is prepared in limited quantity each evening. That the wine list changes based on what your importers have that you believe in. None of that is apologetic. All of it is a promise — a very specific promise that a certain kind of guest will recognize as the reason they want to come.

You used a phrase just now that stuck with me: "thirty-eight is where we're honest." That's actually the most useful single sentence you've said, and it might be the sentence the paragraph is built around. Not quite those words — that's your internal shorthand — but that idea. The restaurant is built around a very particular idea of what honesty looks like in a kitchen and a dining room, and the size is an expression of that, not an accident of it.

Is there anyone you trust — outside the restaurant, outside your importer relationships — who you'd want to read a draft of that paragraph before it goes up? Sometimes it helps to have one person who can tell you when you've slipped into the language of trying too hard.

My wife, Yuki. She has no professional stake in the restaurant — she works in publishing, she has a very calibrated ear for when something is written to impress versus written to communicate. She'll tell me immediately if it sounds like I'm trying too hard. She was the one who read the Asahi Shimbun Weekly headline out loud to me Thursday morning because I literally couldn't look at my phone. She said it very quietly, like she knew she was handing me something fragile. "Azabu's Quiet Modena: A Trattoria With Conviction." She read it twice and then just waited.

I think that's going to stay with me for a long time. Not just the review, not just what Hiroko Sano wrote about the ragu bolognese and the wine list and the unfussy precision — all of that matters enormously — but that specific moment of Yuki reading the headline quietly while I held my breath. That's the context around everything else we've talked about today. The ragu conversation with Takashi on Tuesday, the call with the importer, the paragraph for the website — all of it is downstream of that one Thursday morning moment.

I think I actually know what I need to do. I came into this conversation feeling overwhelmed. I feel something different now. Not less scared exactly, but like the fear has a shape.

"The fear has a shape" — that's exactly what it means to have moved from panic to a plan. You came in holding something large and formless, and now you're holding several specific things with edges you can work with.

Let me reflect back what you've landed on, because it's worth hearing it as a coherent whole rather than as a list of tasks.

You're holding the line at thirty-eight covers, not as a constraint you're apologizing for, but as a deliberate expression of what the restaurant is. The demand surge that followed the March 19, 2026 Asahi Shimbun Weekly piece — the 4x spike in reservation requests, the three-week wait for Friday and Saturday dinner — that's not pressure to expand. It's confirmation that what you built at that size is exactly what it's supposed to be.

You're going to cook the ragu bolognese with Takashi on Tuesday morning and do the thing you've been postponing emotionally: translate what you know in your hands into language he can carry. That's not giving away authorship. That's completing the dish — making it robust enough to exist without requiring your constant presence to hold it together.

You're calling your importers tomorrow to have an honest conversation about what the next few months look like, so that the wine list Hiroko Sano described remains the wine list, rather than quietly becoming something more convenient and less itself.

And you're going to write a paragraph — vetted by Yuki — that describes the restaurant plainly, without performance, so that the people arriving because of the review know what they're walking into and arrive ready to receive it.

That's a complete and honest response to a extraordinary week. Not a pivot. Not a scale-up. A deepening.

The moment you described — Yuki reading "Azabu's Quiet Modena: A Trattoria With Conviction" quietly while you held your breath — that's the kind of moment that doesn't need anything added to it. It just needs to be remembered accurately, which it sounds like you already know how to do.

Tuesday with Takashi and the ragu. Let me know how it goes.
